text:
HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) must get your tax return and any money you owe by the deadline.

If you do not know your profit for the whole tax year, you still need to send a tax return. Check how to send a return if you do not know your profit for the whole year.

The last tax year started on 6 April 2025. It ended on 5 April 2026. The deadline for earlier tax returns has passed. You may have to pay a penalty. Send your tax return or payment as soon as you can. This helps you avoid more penalties.

## Telling HMRC you need to complete a return

You must tell HMRC by 5 October if you need to complete a tax return for the previous year. This applies if you:

- have not sent a tax return before

- registered before but did not need to send a tax return for the tax year 2024 to 2025

You can tell HMRC by registering for Self Assessment. Check how to register for Self Assessment.

### If you register after 5 October 2026

HMRC will send you a letter or email. It will give you a different deadline to send your tax return. The deadline is 3 months from the date on the letter or email.

You must still pay the tax you owe by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027. If you do not, you will get a penalty.

## Sending a paper tax return

HMRC must receive your paper tax return by 11:59pm on 31 October 2026. If it arrives late, you'll get a late filing penalty.

You can send it on or after 6 April 2026. HMRC must still receive it by the deadline.

## Submitting an online tax return

You must send your online tax return by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027. If you are late, you will get a late filing penalty.

If you want to pay your Self Assessment bill through your tax code, you must send your return by 11:59pm on 30 December 2026. If you miss this deadline, you will have to pay another way.

You can send your return at any time from 6 April 2026 up to the deadline.

## Paying the tax you owe

You must pay your Self Assessment tax by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027. If you pay late, you will get a penalty.

There is a second payment deadline of 31 July. This applies if you make payments towards your bill. These are called ‘payments on account’.

You can estimate your Self Assessment tax bill before you send your tax return. This can:

- give you an idea of what your bill is likely to be
- help you budget and pay on time

Find help on understanding the tax you owe.

## Trustees of a registered pension scheme or non-resident companies

HMRC must get a paper tax return by 31 January 2027. You cannot send it online.

You can send it on or after 6 April 2026. HMRC must still get it by the deadline.

## Partnership returns if you have a company as a partner

If your partnership's accounting date is between 1 February and 5 April, and one of your partners is a limited company, the deadline is:

- 12 months from the accounting date for online returns
- 9 months from the accounting date for paper returns

You may get a penalty if you need to send a tax return and you:

- send your return late
- pay your tax bill late

You can estimate your penalty for late Self Assessment tax returns and payments.

## If you register for Self Assessment late

If you register after 5 October, and you do not pay all of your tax bill by 31 January, you may get a 'failure to notify' penalty.

The penalty is based on the amount you still have to pay. You will get it within 12 months after HMRC receives your Self Assessment tax return.

You can find more information on 'failure to notify' penalties.

## If you send your tax return late

You will get a penalty if you send your tax return late. There are four steps:

- An initial penalty of £100.
- After 3 months, daily penalties of £10 per day, up to a maximum of £900.
- After 6 months, a further penalty of 5% of the tax due or £300, whichever is higher.
- After 12 months, another penalty of 5% or £300, whichever is higher.

To avoid these penalties, send your Self Assessment tax return as soon as you can.

All partners will be charged a penalty if a partnership tax return is late.

## If you pay your tax late

You will get penalties if you pay late. The penalty is 5% of the tax you have not paid. You get this penalty at:

- 30 days
- 6 months
- 12 months

You will also be charged interest on the amount you owe. To avoid this, pay your Self Assessment tax bill as soon as you can.

Find out what happens if you do not pay your tax bill.

Your State Pension amount depends on your National Insurance record.

Check your State Pension forecast to find out how much you could get when you reach State Pension age. It also shows your National Insurance record.

The full rate of new State Pension is £241.30 a week. Your amount could be different. It depends on:

- if you were contracted out before 2016
- the number of National Insurance qualifying years you have
- if you paid into the Additional State Pension before 2016

Find out what tax you might pay on your retirement income. This includes if you retire abroad.

## If you’re getting less than £241.30 a week

You might need more National Insurance qualifying years to increase your State Pension.

### If your National Insurance record started before April 2016

You may have been contracted out. When you were contracted out, you or your employer paid more into your workplace or private pension. You paid less into your State Pension.

If you were contracted out, you will usually need more than 35 qualifying years. You need this to get the full rate of new State Pension.

### If your National Insurance record started after April 2016

If your National Insurance record started after April 2016, you will need 35 qualifying years. You need this to get the full rate of new State Pension.

## If you're getting more than £241.30 a week

If you paid into the Additional State Pension before 2016, you might get more State Pension under the old rules. If so, you'll get a 'protected payment'. This is paid on top of the full rate of new State Pension.

## Annual increases

The new State Pension goes up each year. It goes up by whichever of these is the highest:

- earnings – the average percentage growth in wages (in Great Britain)

- prices – the percentage growth in prices in the UK, measured by the Consumer Prices Index (CPI)

- 2.5%

If you have a protected payment, it goes up each year in line with the CPI.

There are 2 Child Benefit rates.

| Who the allowance is for | Rate (weekly) |

| Eldest or only child | £27.05 |

| Additional children | £17.90 per child |

If you are paid too much or too little, you must contact the Child Benefit Office.

Child Benefit counts towards the benefit cap. If the cap affects you, you will still get the full amount of Child Benefit. But your other benefits may be reduced.

## If families split up

If a family splits up, you get £27.05 a week for the eldest child.

If you have 2 children and one lives with you and the other lives with someone else (for example, your ex-partner), you'll each get £27.05 a week.

If you both claim for the same child, only one of you will get Child Benefit for them.

If you're entitled to Child Benefit for any other children, you'll get £17.90 for each child.

## If families join together

If you move in with a partner who also claims Child Benefit, you get £27.05 for the eldest child in the household. You get £17.90 for any younger children.

You and your partner can claim for different children. But if you live together, you cannot both claim at the higher rate. You may have to pay back some of the money if you do.

You must report the change to your family circumstances.

## If you or your partner earn over the threshold

You may have to pay the High Income Child Benefit Charge. This applies if your adjusted net income or your partner's adjusted net income is over the threshold.

Your adjusted net income is your total taxable income. It is worked out before any personal allowances. Then you take away things like Gift Aid. Your total taxable income includes interest from savings and dividends.

If you have to pay the charge, you can still get the other advantages of Child Benefit. These include National Insurance credits. The charge cannot be more than the Child Benefit payments you get.

Use the Child Benefit tax calculator to check if your adjusted net income is over the threshold. If it is, the calculator will also tell you how much charge you must pay.

If you and your partner both have an individual income over the threshold, the person with the higher adjusted net income pays the charge.

If you or your partner has an individual income of £20,000 or more above the threshold (£10,000 or more before April 2024), you will be charged the same amount as your Child Benefit payments. So you will get no extra money from Child Benefit.

You can make a claim to opt out of getting payments if you do not want to pay the charge. You can still get the other advantages of Child Benefit, like National Insurance credits.

## If you're under 16

You can claim for yourself. Or someone responsible for you can claim for you. You'll usually get more if you claim yourself.

Universal Credit is paid every month. How much you get depends on:

- your standard allowance
- any extra amounts that apply to you
- any money taken off your payment
- if you're working, how much you earn

You can use a benefits calculator to see how much you could get.

If you get Universal Credit, you'll earn Class 3 National Insurance credits. These count towards your State Pension.

## Standard allowance

You get one standard allowance for your household.

| How much you'll get | Monthly standard allowance |
| If you're single and under 25 | £338.58 |
| If you're single and 25 or over | £424.90 |
| If you live with your partner and you're both under 25 | £528.34 (for you both) |
| If you live with your partner and either of you is 25 or over | £666.97 (for you both) |

## Extra amounts

You may get more money on top of your standard allowance if you’re eligible.

You will need to tell us when you become eligible for an extra amount. They are not added automatically. For example, if you become a carer you need to tell DWP. The carer’s element of Universal Credit is not automatically added if you start getting Carer’s Allowance.

### If you have children

You’ll get £303.94 a month for each child who lives with you.

If your first child was born before 6 April 2017, you’ll get an extra £47.94 a month for that child.

You get money for each child until 31 August after their:

- 16th birthday

- 19th birthday, if they’re in eligible education or training. For example, they’re studying for GCSEs, A levels, BTECs, Scottish Highers or SVQs or NVQs up to level 3.

### If your child has a disability

You might get an extra monthly amount if any of your children are disabled.

You’ll either get:

- £164.79 – the lower amount

- £514.71 – the higher amount

The higher amount is for a child who:

- gets the highest rate of the care component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children

- gets the higher rate of the daily living part of Personal Independence Payment (PIP)

- is blind or severely sight impaired

The lower amount is for a child who gets any other rate of either DLA for children, or PIP.

### Childcare costs

You can claim back up to 85% of your childcare costs if you’re working. If you live with your partner, you both need to be working. This does not apply if one of you cannot work because of a disability or health condition.

The childcare must be from a registered provider. You can get help paying for childcare, including nurseries, childminders, breakfast clubs, after school care and holiday clubs.

The most you can get each month is:

- £1,071.09 for one child

- £1,836.16 for 2 or more children

You need to pay your childcare costs up front. Then you claim the money back as part of your payment. You can get support to help you pay your childcare costs up front. Talk to your work coach after you’ve made your claim.

Read more about childcare costs and Universal Credit.

### If you have a disability or health condition

You might get an extra monthly amount if you cannot work because of a health condition, disability or long-term illness.

| How much you’ll get | Extra monthly amount |

| If you have a severe health condition or disability that’s unlikely to change or you are nearing the end of your life | £429.80 |

| If your health condition or disability is assessed as less severe or your condition may improve over time | £217.26 |

There are different rules if you reported a health condition before 6 April 2026.

If you live with your partner and you both have limited capability for work and work-related activity, you’ll only get one extra monthly amount. You’ll get the higher amount if one of you is eligible for it.

If you get the severe disability premium and you’re moving to Universal Credit, you might also be entitled to a ‘transitional protection’ payment.

Read more about health conditions, disability and Universal Credit.

### If you care for someone who gets a health or disability-related benefit

You could get an extra amount known as a ‘carer’s element’. It is added to your Universal Credit if you care for someone who gets one of the following benefits:

- Adult Disability Payment – standard or enhanced award

- Armed Forces Independence Payment

- Attendance Allowance

- Child Disability Payment – middle or highest care award

- Constant Attendance Allowance – full day rate, intermediate rate or exceptional rate with Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit

- Constant Attendance Allowance – full day rate with a War Disablement Pension

- Disability Living Allowance – middle or highest care rate

- Personal Independence Payment – either rate of the daily living part

You need to care for them for at least 35 hours a week.

You’ll get an extra monthly amount of £209.34. If you live with your partner and you both care for the same person, you’ll only get one extra monthly amount.

You may also be eligible for Carer’s Allowance.

This is on top of any extra amount you get if you have a disabled child.

If you are getting an extra amount because you have limited capability for work and work-related activity (LCWRA), you cannot also get the carer’s element.

If the person you care for gets the severe disability premium, it will stop when you claim the carer’s element of Universal Credit.

### Housing costs

You could get money to help pay your housing costs. The payment can cover rent and some service charges.

If you’re a homeowner, you might be able to get a loan to help with interest payments on your mortgage.

## Money taken off your payment

Your payment might go down if any of these things apply to you:

-

you are paying back an advance on a Universal Credit payment

-

you would get more than the amount set by the benefit cap

-

you have been paid too much benefit in the past

-

you owe money for Council Tax, court fines, electricity, gas, water or Child Maintenance

-

you pay your gas or electricity bill from your Universal Credit payment

-

you have a job that pays you

-

you have other money coming in. For example, money from pensions or some other benefits.

-

you have more than £6,000 in money, savings and investments

If you have over £6,000 in money, savings and investments, your payment goes down by £4.35 for every £250 you have between £6,000 and £16,000. Another £4.35 is taken off for any money left over that is not a full £250.

Find out more about money taken off your Universal Credit payment.

### Benefits that affect how much Universal Credit you get

You can get Universal Credit at the same time as other benefits. Your Universal Credit payment goes down by the same amount as the other benefit payment. This applies if you get Universal Credit and any of these benefits:

- Armed Forces Pensions

- Carer’s Allowance

- Carer Support Payment (Scotland)

- Incapacity Benefit

- Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit (not including any increases where constant attendance is needed, or for exceptionally severe disablement)

- Maternity Allowance

- Severe Disablement Allowance

- State Pension

- Widowed Mother’s Allowance

- Widowed Parent’s Allowance

- New Style Employment and Support Allowance (ESA)

- New Style Jobseeker’s Allowance (JSA)

## Claiming Universal Credit and New Style ESA or JSA

You may be able to get Universal Credit and New Style ESA or JSA at the same time. If you do, your Universal Credit payment goes down. It goes down by the amount you get for New Style ESA or JSA.

New Style ESA and JSA are paid more often than Universal Credit.

You also get different National Insurance credits. These count towards your State Pension. They can also help you qualify for other benefits.

You may still get New Style ESA or JSA if your situation changes. Your Universal Credit payment may go down or stop. For example, this could happen if:

- your partner's income goes up

- you have more than £16,000 in savings

Check if you can get:

- New Style Jobseeker's Allowance

- New Style Employment and Support Allowance

## Moving to Universal Credit from other benefits

If you have applied for Universal Credit, you will keep getting your current benefit for 2 more weeks. You must still be eligible for your current benefit.

This only applies if you get income-related Employment and Support Allowance or Housing Benefit.

You do not have to pay back the extra payments. They will not affect the Universal Credit you might get.

If you have received a Migration Notice letter telling you to claim Universal Credit, you might also get a 'transitional protection' payment.

## If your Universal Credit claim is reviewed

Your claim might be reviewed. This makes sure you get the right payment and support.

Find out more about Universal Credit reviews.
You may be able to get Carer's Allowance. You may qualify if you meet certain rules. The person you care for must also meet rules. The care you give must meet rules too.

## The person you care for

The person you care for must already get one of these benefits:

- Personal Independence Payment - daily living component
- Disability Living Allowance - the middle or highest care rate
- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance - the middle or highest care rate
- Attendance Allowance
- Pension Age Disability Payment
- Constant Attendance Allowance at or above the normal maximum rate with an Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit
- Constant Attendance Allowance at the basic (full day) rate with a War Disablement Pension
- Armed Forces Independence Payment
- Child Disability Payment - the middle or highest care rate
- Adult Disability Payment - daily living component at the standard or enhanced rate

### If you care for the person with others

You cannot get Carer's Allowance if you share the care of someone and the other carer is already claiming:

- Carer's Allowance for that person
- Carer Support Payment for that person
- the extra amount of Universal Credit for caring for someone who gets a disability-related benefit for that person

If you want to get Carer's Allowance, speak to the other carer. Ask them about changing their benefits.

If the other carer does not want to do that, you can still apply for Carer's Allowance. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) will decide who should receive the benefit.

## The type of care you provide

You need to spend at least 35 hours a week caring for someone. This can include:

- helping with washing and cooking
- taking the person you care for to a doctor's appointment
- helping with household tasks, like paying bills and shopping

## Your eligibility

All of the following must apply:

- you’re 16 or over

- you spend at least 35 hours a week caring for someone

- you’ve been in England, Scotland or Wales for at least 2 of the last 3 years (this does not apply if you’re a refugee or have humanitarian protection status)

- you normally live in England or Wales, or you live abroad as a member of the armed forces (you might still be eligible if you’re moving to or already living in an EEA country or Switzerland)

- you’re not in full-time education

- you’re not studying for 21 hours a week or more

- you’re not subject to immigration control

- your earnings are £204 or less a week after tax, National Insurance and expenses

If you live in Scotland, you need to apply for Carer Support Payment. You cannot apply for Carer’s Allowance.

If you’re from the EU, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland or Liechtenstein, you and your family usually also need settled or pre-settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme. You need this to get Carer’s Allowance. The deadline to apply to the scheme was 30 June 2021 for most people. You might still be able to apply. Check if you can still apply to the EU Settlement Scheme.

### Calculating your earnings

Your earnings are any income from employment and self-employment. This is after tax, National Insurance and expenses.

Expenses can include:

- 50% of your pension contributions

- equipment you need to do your job, for example specialist clothing

- travel costs between different workplaces. Your employer must not pay for these. For example, fuel or train fares

- business costs if you’re self-employed, for example a computer you only use for work

If you pay a carer to look after the disabled person or your children while you work, you can treat some care costs as an expense. This works if the costs are less than or equal to 50% of your earnings. The carer must not be your spouse, partner, parent, child or sibling.

Example

You earn £100 a week. This is after tax, National Insurance and other expenses. You spend £60 a week on care while you work. You can treat £50 of this as an expense.

These payments do not count as earnings:

- money received from an occupational or private pension

- contributions towards your living or accommodation costs from someone you live with. They cannot be a tenant or boarder.

- the first £20 a week and 50% of the rest of any income you make from someone boarding in your home

- a loan or advance payment from your employer

## If you get State Pension

You cannot get the full amount of both Carer's Allowance and your State Pension at the same time.

If your pension is £86.45 a week or more, you will not get a Carer's Allowance payment.

If your pension is less than £86.45 a week, you will get a Carer's Allowance payment. It will make up the difference.

## If you get Pension Credit

If your State Pension is more than £86.45 a week, you will not get a Carer's Allowance payment. Your Pension Credit payments will go up instead.

Pension Credit tops up:

- your weekly income to £238 if you're single

- your joint weekly income to £363.25 if you have a partner

You may get extra amounts if you have other responsibilities and costs.

The top up and extra amounts are known as 'Guarantee Credit'.

## If you have a severe disability

You could get an extra £86.05 a week if you get any of the following:

- Attendance Allowance
- the middle or highest rate of the care component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA)
- the daily living component of Personal Independence Payment (PIP)
- Armed Forces Independence Payment
- the daily living component of Adult Disability Payment
- Pension Age Disability Payment
- the middle or highest rate of the care component of Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance

## If you care for another adult

You could get an extra £48.15 a week if:

- you get Carer's Allowance

- you get Carer Support Payment

- you've claimed Carer's Allowance but are not being paid because you already get another benefit paying a higher amount

If you and your partner have both claimed or are getting Carer's Allowance, you can both get this extra amount.

## If you're responsible for children or young people

You could get an extra amount for each child or young person you're responsible for. They must live with you.

You'll get £69.98 a week for each child or young person. This goes up to £81.07 a week for the first child. This applies if they were born before 6 April 2017.

You will get the extra amount until 31 August after their:

- 16th birthday

- 19th birthday, if they're in eligible education or training. For example, they're studying for GCSEs, A levels, BTECs, Scottish Highers or SVQs or NVQs up to level 3.

If they're in education, it must be more than 12 hours a week on average.

### If the child or young person is disabled

You could also get an extra amount if the child or young person is disabled.

You could get an extra £37.93 a week if the child or young person gets:

- Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children. They must get the lowest or middle rate of the care component, or any rate of the mobility component.

- Child Disability Payment. They must get the lowest or middle rate of the care component, or any rate of the mobility component.

- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance. They must get the lowest or middle rate of the care component, or any rate of the mobility component.

- Personal Independence Payment (PIP). They must get the standard rate of the daily living component, or any rate of the mobility component.

- Adult Disability Payment. They must get the standard rate of the daily living component, or any rate of the mobility component.

You could get an extra £118.46 a week if the child or young person gets:

- Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children. They must get the highest rate of the care component.

- Child Disability Payment. They must get the highest rate of the care component.

- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance. They must get the highest rate of the care component.

- Personal Independence Payment (PIP). They must get the enhanced rate of the daily living component.

- Adult Disability Payment. They must get the enhanced rate of the daily living component.

You might also be eligible if they're blind or severely sight impaired.

## If you have housing costs

You could get an extra amount to cover your housing costs. These costs can include:

- ground rent if your property is a leasehold

- some service charges

- charges for tents and site rents

The amount you could get depends on your housing costs.

If you get Pension Credit, you could also be eligible for:

- Council Tax Reduction

- Housing Benefit if you rent the property you live in

- Support for Mortgage Interest if you own the property you live in

## If you have savings or a second pension

You could get the 'Savings Credit' part of Pension Credit. This is true if both of these apply:

- you reached State Pension age before 6 April 2016
- you saved some money for retirement, for example in a personal or workplace pension

You'll get up to £17.96 Savings Credit a week if you're single. If you have a partner, you'll get up to £20.10 a week.

You might still get some Savings Credit. This can happen even if you do not get the Guarantee Credit part of Pension Credit.

## Other help if you get Pension Credit

If you get Pension Credit, you will automatically get cold weather payments.

You can also:

-
apply for a free TV licence if you are aged 75 or over

-
get help with NHS costs if you get the Guarantee Credit part of Pension Credit

NHS costs can include things like prescriptions, dental treatment, glasses and transport costs for hospital appointments.

## Get help with extra amounts

Call the Pension Service helpline if you are not sure whether you can get extra amounts.

Pension Service helpline

Telephone: 0800 99 1234

Relay UK (if you cannot hear or speak on the phone): 18001 then 0800 99 1234

British Sign Language (BSL) video relay service if you are on a computer. Find out how to use the service on a mobile or tablet.

Monday to Friday, 8am to 6pm. Closed on public holidays.

Find out about call charges.

Statutory Maternity Pay (SMP) is paid for up to 39 weeks. You get:

- 90% of your average weekly earnings (before tax) for the first 6 weeks.
- £194.32 or 90% of your average weekly earnings, whichever is lower, for the next 33 weeks.

SMP is paid the same way as your wages. For example, it may be paid monthly or weekly. Tax and National Insurance will be taken off.

Use the maternity planner to help you work out how much maternity pay you could get.

If you take Shared Parental Leave, you'll get Statutory Shared Parental Pay (ShPP). ShPP is £194.32 a week. It is 90% of your average weekly earnings if that is lower.

## Start date

Statutory Maternity Pay (SMP) usually starts when you take your maternity leave.

It starts automatically if you are off work with a pregnancy-related illness in the 4 weeks before the week your baby is due. The week runs from Sunday to Saturday.

## Problems and disputes

Ask your employer to explain your SMP if you think it's not right. If you disagree about the amount, or your employer cannot pay, contact the Statutory Payment Disputes Team. Your employer might not be able to pay if they are insolvent.

If you’re eligible, you can get £123.25 a week Statutory Sick Pay (SSP). You can also get 80% of your normal weekly earnings. You get whichever is lower. It’s paid for up to 28 weeks.

You’ll be paid SSP for all the full days you’re off sick. These are the days you would normally have worked.

Your employer will use your average weekly earnings over an 8-week period. They use this to work out how much you get. You still qualify if you started your job recently. This is true even if you have not yet received 8 weeks’ pay. Ask your employer to find out more.

## How you're paid

Your employer pays SSP. They pay it the same way as your normal wages. For example, this might be weekly or monthly.

If you have more than one job, you may get SSP from each employer.

Tax and National Insurance will be taken off.

If you think you're not getting the right amount of SSP, talk to your employer. If you still think it's wrong, contact the HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) enquiry line.

The hourly rate depends on your age. It also depends on whether you are an apprentice.

This page is also available in Welsh (Cymraeg).

You must be at least:

- school leaving age to get the National Minimum Wage
- aged 21 to get the National Living Wage. The minimum wage still applies to workers aged 20 and under.

## Current rates

The rates change on 1 April every year.

| | 21 and over | 18 to 20 | Under 18 | Apprentice |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| April 2026 | £12.71 | £10.85 | £8 | £8 |
| April 2027 | £13.21 | £11.27 | £8.31 | £8.31 |

### Apprentices

An apprentice gets the apprentice rate if they are either:

- under 19
- 19 or over and in the first year of their apprenticeship

Example

An apprentice aged 21 in the first year of their apprenticeship gets a minimum hourly rate of £8.

An apprentice gets the minimum wage for their age if they both:

- are 19 or over
- have finished the first year of their apprenticeship

Example

An apprentice aged 21 who has finished the first year of their apprenticeship gets a minimum hourly rate of £12.71.

## Previous rates

These rates were for the National Living Wage and the National Minimum Wage from April 2019.

### Rates between 1 April 2024 and 31 March 2026

The National Living Wage has applied to people aged 21 and over since 1 April 2024.

| | 21 and over | 18 to 20 | Under 18 | Apprentice |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| April 2025 to March 2026 | £12.21 | £10 | £7.55 | £7.55 |
| April 2024 to March 2025 | £11.44 | £8.60 | £6.40 | £6.40 |

### Rates between 1 April 2021 and 31 March 2024

From 1 April 2021 to 31 March 2024, the National Living Wage applied to people aged 23 and over.

| | 23 and over | 21 to 22 | 18 to 20 | Under 18 | Apprentice |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| April 2023 to March 2024 | £10.42 | £10.18 | £7.49 | £5.28 | £5.28 |
| April 2022 to March 2023 | £9.50 | £9.18 | £6.83 | £4.81 | £4.81 |
| April 2021 to March 2022 | £8.91 | £8.36 | £6.56 | £4.62 | £4.30 |

### Rates before 1 April 2021

Before 1 April 2021, the National Living Wage applied to people aged 25 and over.

| | 25 and over | 21 to 24 | 18 to 20 | Under 18 | Apprentice |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| April 2020 to March 2021 | £8.72 | £8.20 | £6.45 | £4.55 | £4.15 |
| April 2019 to March 2020 | £8.21 | £7.70 | £6.15 | £4.35 | £3.90 |

## If your income is over £35,000

## If you live alone or no one you live with is eligible for the Winter Fuel Payment

Attendance Allowance is paid weekly. It has 2 rates. The rate you get depends on how much help you need.

Attendance Allowance is not means-tested. This means your earnings and your savings do not affect what you get.

## Attendance Allowance rates

| Rate | Level of help you need |
|---|---|
| Lower rate - £76.70 | Frequent help or constant supervision during the day, or supervision at night |
| Higher rate - £114.60 | Help or supervision throughout both day and night, or a medical professional has said you're nearing the end of life |

Your rate could change if your situation changes. You must tell us about any change in your circumstances.

If you get Attendance Allowance, you might also get more Pension Credit, Housing Benefit or Council Tax Reduction. Check with the helpline or office that deals with your benefit.

You may get Constant Attendance Allowance at the same time. If you do, your Attendance Allowance will go down. It goes down by the amount of Constant Attendance Allowance you get.

How much Personal Independence Payment (PIP) you get depends on how hard you find:

- everyday activities ('daily living' tasks)

- getting around ('mobility' tasks)

Find out which tasks count as daily living and mobility tasks.

## PIP amounts

| | Lower weekly rate | Higher weekly rate |
|---|---|---|
| Daily living part | £76.70 | £114.60 |
| Mobility part | £30.30 | £80 |

PIP is tax free. Your income does not affect the amount you get. Your savings do not affect it either.

Tell the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) straight away if your personal circumstances change. Tell them too if your condition affects you in a different way.

## How you’re paid

PIP is usually paid every 4 weeks.

Your decision letter tells you:

- the date of your first payment
- what day of the week you’ll usually be paid
- how long you’ll get PIP for
- when and if your claim will be reviewed

If your payment date is on a bank holiday, you’ll usually be paid before the bank holiday. After that, you’ll keep getting paid as normal.

Your money is paid into your bank, building society or credit union account. This is the same for all benefits, pensions and allowances.

## Other help you can get

If you get the mobility part of PIP, you might be able to get a:

- Blue Badge
- vehicle tax discount or exemption
- Motability Scheme vehicle, if you get the higher mobility rate of PIP

If you get either the daily living or mobility part of PIP, you can get a Disabled Persons Railcard.

You may be able to get a discount on Council Tax and local bus travel. Contact your local council to check.

If someone helps to care for you, they may be able to get Carer's Allowance or Carer's Credit.

Find out about other financial support for people with disabilities or health conditions.

## If you get other benefits and PIP

You may get a top-up. It is called a disability premium. You may get this if you get:

- income-related Employment and Support Allowance (ESA)

- Housing Benefit

If you get Constant Attendance Allowance, you will get less of the daily living part of PIP.

If you get War Pensioners' Mobility Supplement, you will not get the mobility part of PIP.

Marriage Allowance lets you transfer £1,260 of your Personal Allowance to your husband, wife or civil partner. Your Personal Allowance is the amount you can earn before you pay tax.

This cuts their tax by up to £252 in the tax year. The tax year runs from 6 April to 5 April the next year.

This guide is also available in Welsh (Cymraeg).

To benefit as a couple, you must normally be the lower earner. Your income must be below your Personal Allowance. This is usually £12,570.

You can work out how much tax you could save as a couple.

Call the Income Tax helpline instead if you get other income. This includes dividends, savings or benefits from your job. Also call if you do not know what your taxable income is.

When you transfer some of your Personal Allowance, you might pay more tax yourself. But you could still pay less as a couple.

Example

Your income is £11,500. Your Personal Allowance is £12,570. So you do not pay tax.

Your partner's income is £20,000. Their Personal Allowance is £12,570. So they pay tax on £7,430. This is their 'taxable income'. As a couple, you are paying Income Tax on £7,430.

When you claim Marriage Allowance, you transfer £1,260 of your Personal Allowance to your partner. Your Personal Allowance becomes £11,310. Your partner gets a reduction of £1,260 on their taxable income.

Now you will pay tax on £190. Your partner will only pay tax on £6,170. As a couple, you benefit. You are only paying Income Tax on £6,360, not £7,430. This saves you £214 in tax.

## Who can apply

You can get Marriage Allowance if all of these are true:

- You are married or in a civil partnership.
- You do not pay Income Tax. Or your income is below your Personal Allowance (usually £12,570).
- Your partner pays Income Tax at the basic rate. This usually means their income is between £12,571 and £50,270 before they get Marriage Allowance.

You cannot claim Marriage Allowance if you live together but are not married or in a civil partnership.

If you live in Scotland, your partner must pay the starter, basic or intermediate rate. This usually means their income is between £12,571 and £43,662.

These things will not affect your application for Marriage Allowance if you or your partner:

- are getting a pension
- live abroad, as long as you get a Personal Allowance

If you or your partner were born before 6 April 1935, you might be better off as a couple if you apply for Married Couple’s Allowance instead.

You cannot get Marriage Allowance and Married Couple’s Allowance at the same time.

## Backdating your claim

You can backdate your claim to 6 April 2022. This is the 2022 to 2023 tax year. You can do this for any years you were eligible for Marriage Allowance.

Your partner’s tax bill will go down. How much it goes down depends on the Personal Allowance rate for the years you are backdating.

If your partner has died since 5 April 2022, you can still claim. Phone the Income Tax helpline. If your partner was the lower earner, the person who manages their tax affairs needs to phone.

## Stopping Marriage Allowance

Marriage Allowance moves to your partner each year. It keeps doing this until you cancel it.

You might want to cancel it if your income changes. You might also cancel it if your relationship ends.

You'll normally get statutory redundancy pay if you're an employee. You also need to have worked for your current employer for 2 years or more.

You'll get:

- half a week's pay for each full year you were under 22
- one week's pay for each full year you were 22 or older but under 41
- one and a half weeks' pay for each full year you were 41 or older

Your length of service counts for 20 years at most.

Your weekly pay is the average amount you earned each week in the 12 weeks before the day you got your redundancy notice.

If you were paid less than usual because you were 'on furlough' because of coronavirus, your statutory redundancy pay is based on what you would have earned normally.

If you were made redundant on or after 6 April 2026, your weekly pay is capped at £751. The most statutory redundancy pay you can get is £22,530. If you were made redundant before 6 April 2026, these amounts will be lower.

Calculate your redundancy pay.

You have 6 months from the day your job ends to apply for statutory redundancy pay.

### Exceptions

You do not get statutory redundancy pay if:

- your employer offers to keep you on

- your employer offers you suitable alternative work and you turn it down without good reason

Being dismissed for misconduct is not redundancy. So you would not get statutory redundancy pay if this happened.

You do not get statutory redundancy pay if you fall into one or more of these groups:

- former registered dock workers (covered by other arrangements) and share fishermen

- crown servants, members of the armed forces or police services

- apprentices who are not employees at the end of their training

- a domestic servant who is a member of the employer's immediate family

## Short-term and temporary lay-offs

You can claim statutory redundancy pay if you are eligible. You also need to have been temporarily laid off. This means you had no pay, or less than half a week's pay, for either:

- more than 4 weeks in a row
- more than 6 weeks that were not in a row, within a 13 week period

Write to your employer. Tell them you plan to claim statutory redundancy pay. You must do this within 4 weeks of your last day off work in the 4 or 6 week period.

If your employer does not reject your claim within 7 days, write to them again. Give them your notice.

Your claim could be rejected. This can happen if your normal work is likely to start within 4 weeks. It can also happen if that work will last at least 13 weeks.

How much Income Tax you pay in each tax year depends on:

- how much of your income is above your Personal Allowance

- how much of your income falls within each tax band

Some income is tax-free.

The current tax year runs from 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027.

This guide is also available in Welsh (Cymraeg).

## Your tax-free Personal Allowance

The standard Personal Allowance is £12,570. This is the amount of income you do not have to pay tax on.

### If you earn more than £100,000

Your Personal Allowance goes down. It drops by £1 for every £2 that your adjusted net income is above £100,000. Your allowance is zero if your income is £125,140 or more.

### Blind Person's Allowance

You may be able to earn more before you start paying Income Tax. To do this, you claim Blind Person's Allowance. This tax-free allowance is added to your Personal Allowance.

## Income Tax rates and bands

The table shows the tax rates you pay in each band. This is if you have a standard Personal Allowance of £12,570.

Income tax bands are different if you live in Scotland.

| Band | Taxable income | Tax rate |

| Personal Allowance | Up to £12,570 | 0% |

| Basic rate | £12,571 to £50,270 | 20% |

| Higher rate | £50,271 to £125,140 | 40% |

| Additional rate | over £125,140 | 45% |

You can also see the rates and bands without the Personal Allowance. You do not get a Personal Allowance on taxable income over £125,140.

### If you're employed or get a pension

Check your Income Tax to see:

- your Personal Allowance and tax code
- how much tax you've paid in the current tax year
- how much you're likely to pay for the rest of the year

## Other allowances

You have tax-free allowances for:

- savings interest

- dividend income, if you own shares in a company

You may also have tax-free allowances for:

- your first £1,000 of income from self-employment. This is your ‘trading allowance’.

- your first £1,000 of income from property you rent. This does not apply if you use the Rent a Room Scheme.

Find out if you can get the trading and property allowances.

You pay tax on any interest, dividends or income over your allowances.

## Paying less Income Tax

You can also pay less tax through tax reliefs, if you qualify. For example:

- charity donations
- job expenses
- private pension contributions
- maintenance payments

### If you're married or in a civil partnership

You may be able to claim Marriage Allowance. This can reduce your partner's tax. You can claim it if your income is less than the standard Personal Allowance.

If you do not claim Marriage Allowance, you may be able to claim Married Couple's Allowance. You may be able to claim it if you or your partner were born before 6 April 1935.

You may pay a different rate of tax on gains from businesses than on other assets.

You do not usually pay tax when you sell your home.

From 6 April 2026, you’ll pay Income Tax and National Insurance contributions on carried interest you receive instead.

## If you pay higher rate Income Tax

If you pay higher or additional rate Income Tax, you pay 24% on your gains from 6 April 2026.

You can see the rates and allowance for earlier years.

## If you pay basic rate Income Tax

If you are a basic rate taxpayer, the rate you pay on gains you receive from 6 April 2026 depends on two things.

- The size of your gain.
- Your taxable income.

You can see the rates and allowance for previous years.

To work out your rate:

- Work out how much taxable income you have. This is your income minus your Personal Allowance. Then take away any other Income Tax reliefs you are entitled to.

- Work out your total taxable gains.

- Take your tax-free allowance away from your total taxable gains.

- Add this amount to your taxable income.

- If this amount is within the basic Income Tax band, you pay 18% on your gains made from 6 April 2026.

- For any amount above the basic Income Tax band, you pay 24% on gains made from 6 April 2026.

### Example 1

You make a gain on or after 6 April 2026. Your taxable income is £20,000. This is your income minus your Personal Allowance and any Income Tax reliefs. Your taxable gains are £12,600.

First, take the Capital Gains tax-free allowance away from your taxable gain. For the 2026 to 2027 tax year, the allowance is £3,000. This leaves £9,600 to pay tax on.

Add this to your taxable income. The total is £29,600. This is less than £37,700, the basic rate band for the 2026 to 2027 tax year. So you pay Capital Gains Tax at 18%.

This means you pay £1,728 in Capital Gains Tax.

### Example 2

You make a gain on or after 6 April 2026. Your taxable income is £20,000. This is your income minus your Personal Allowance and any Income Tax reliefs. Your taxable gains are £52,600.

First, take the Capital Gains tax-free allowance away from your taxable gain. For the 2026 to 2027 tax year, the allowance is £3,000. This leaves £49,600 to pay tax on.

Add this to your taxable income. The total is £69,600. This is more than £37,700, the basic rate band for the 2026 to 2027 tax year. So you pay Capital Gains Tax at 18% on £17,700. Then you pay 24% on £31,900.

This means you will pay £10,842.

## If you’re a trustee, personal representative or business

Trustees or personal representatives pay tax on someone’s gains after they have died. The rate is 24% from 6 April 2026.

You can see the rates and allowance for previous years.

### If you qualify for Business Asset Disposal Relief

From 6 April 2026, the rate is 18% if you are a sole trader, partnership or trustee. This applies if your gains qualify for Business Asset Disposal Relief.

You can see the rates and allowance for previous years.

### If you have gains charged at more than one rate

You can use your tax-free allowance against the gains taxed at the highest rates. For example, you might pay 24% on some gains and 18% on others.

You can see the rates and allowance for previous years.

Inheritance Tax is a tax on the estate of someone who has died. The estate is the property, money and possessions they leave behind.

You normally do not have to pay Inheritance Tax if either of these is true:

- Your estate is worth less than the £325,000 threshold.
- You leave everything above the £325,000 threshold to your spouse, civil partner, a charity or a community amateur sports club.

You may still have to report the value of the estate. This is true even if it is below the threshold.

If you give your home to your children or grandchildren, your threshold can go up to £500,000. Children include adopted, foster and stepchildren.

If you are married or in a civil partnership, and your estate is worth less than your threshold, your partner's threshold can go up. It goes up by any part of your threshold that you did not use. This happens when you die.

This guide is also available in Welsh (Cymraeg).

## Inheritance Tax rates

The standard Inheritance Tax rate is 40%. You only pay it on the part of your estate above the threshold.

### Example

Your estate is worth £500,000. Your tax-free threshold is £325,000. The part above the threshold is £175,000. That is £500,000 minus £325,000. Inheritance Tax is 40% of £175,000.

The estate can pay a lower rate of 36% on some assets. This applies if you leave 10% or more of the 'net value' to charity in your will. The net value is the estate's total value minus any debts.

### Reliefs and exemptions

Some gifts you give while you are alive may be taxed after you die. 'Taper relief' may lower the tax on a gift. It depends on when you gave the gift. The tax may then be less than 40%.

Other reliefs exist. Business Relief and Agricultural Relief are two examples. They let some assets pass on with no Inheritance Tax. They also let some assets pass on with a smaller bill.

## Who pays the tax to HMRC

Money from your estate pays Inheritance Tax to HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC). The person dealing with the estate does this. This person is called the ‘executor’ if there is a will.

Your beneficiaries are the people who inherit your estate. They do not normally pay tax on what they inherit. They may have other taxes to pay. For example, this can happen if they get rent from a house left to them in a will.

People you give gifts to might have to pay Inheritance Tax. This only happens if you give away more than £325,000 and die within 7 years.
